title: Saving media and transcripts
summary: Save audio/video with selectable subtitles, or export a separate transcript.
body:
Right-click an audio/video source in the Document Explorer, or right-click its open player, audio placeholder, or transcript. Choose **Save with Transcript…**. The explorer exports the selected source even when a different source is open. In the save dialog, choose the file type: **Media copy with selectable subtitles** creates a Matroska video (.mkv) or audio (.mka) file; **Plain text** saves the words; **SubRip (.srt)** and **WebVTT (.vtt)** save timed subtitles.

Media export requires FFmpeg installed locally. It copies the audio/video tracks without re-encoding and adds the stored transcript as a selectable subtitle track. Use a player that supports Matroska subtitles; captions are not burned into the picture. Existing subtitle tracks are replaced in the exported copy by this transcript. The original source is never overwritten. Transcript-only exports do not require FFmpeg.

Saving runs in the background and can be cancelled in the process monitor. Failed or cancelled exports do not replace an existing destination. The player action is disabled until transcript segments are available. The explorer action reads the selected source’s saved transcript in the background and reports if no transcript is available yet. No transcription or model call is rerun. Bind **Save with Transcript** in Settings → Shortcuts to use it while the media viewer has focus.

title: What is Papyrus?
summary: An overview of every major feature and how they fit together.
body:
# Welcome to Papyrus

Papyrus is an AI-powered research assistant for PDF documents. It combines a PDF reader, structured knowledge extraction, a visual workspace, conversational AI, and a fully programmable workflow engine into one application.

## The core loop

1. **Import PDFs** — add documents to a project.
2. **Read & annotate** — highlight passages, write notes, assign tags.
3. **Analyze** — run an AI analysis template to extract claims, arguments, or entities as a graph.
4. **Explore** — review extracted nodes in the Workspace canvas or the Analysis review panel.
5. **Chat** — ask follow-up questions; the AI has context from all your indexed documents.
6. **Build workflows** — automate repetitive tasks with the Blueprint Editor.

## Major features at a glance

| Feature | Where to find it |
|---|---|
| PDF reader | Main viewer area |
| Highlights & notes | Right-click selected text |
| Document Analysis | Research dock → 🔬 Analysis tab |
| Chat with documents | Research dock → 💬 Chat tab |
| Brainstorm | Research dock → 💡 Brainstorm tab |
| Research Agent | Research dock → 🧭 Research Agent tab |
| Custom tool builder | Research dock → 🛠️ Blueprint Editor tab |
| Knowledge Workspace | Workspace dock |
| Tags & organisation | Toolbar → Tag Manager |
| Prompt editor | Toolbar → Prompt Editor (🧠) |
| Text-to-speech | Toolbar → Other Tools → Audio |
| OCR | Right-click a document in explorer |
| Dictionary | Toolbar → Other Tools → Dictionary |
| Prompt tracing | Each AI response card → View Prompt Trace |

## Projects

Everything lives inside a **project** (`.pdfproj` file). Open or create one before you start. Papyrus auto-saves as you work.

## Getting help

- Press **F1** with any panel focused to open help for that control.
- Press **Shift+F1** to activate What's This? mode — then click any element.
- Use **Help → Help Center** to browse or search all topics.
- Use **Help → Interactive Tutorials** for step-by-step walkthroughs.

title: Creating and Opening Projects
summary: How to create a new project, open an existing one, and understand what a project stores.
body:
# Projects

A Papyrus project is a single `.pdfproj` file (a SQLite database) that stores everything: your PDF list, highlights, notes, tags, workspace graphs, analysis results, chat history, and AI settings.

## Create a new project

1. Click the **Project (📁)** button in the top toolbar.
2. Select **New Project**.
3. Choose a save location and enter a name. Papyrus creates the `.pdfproj` file there.

Tip: Keep your `.pdfproj` file in the same folder as your PDFs for easy portability.

## Open an existing project

1. Click **Project (📁) → Open Project**.
2. Browse to a `.pdfproj` file and open it.

Recent projects appear at the top of the Project menu for one-click access.

## Save your project

Papyrus auto-saves as you work. You can also:
- Click the **Save (💾)** button in the toolbar for an explicit save.
- Use **Project → Save Project As** to save a copy to a different location.

## What a project stores

- All imported PDF file paths (the PDFs themselves are not copied in)
- Highlights and annotation notes
- Tags and tag assignments
- Workspace graph nodes and edges
- All AI analysis results
- Chat history for each session
- Analysis template customisations
- Project-level AI settings
- Blueprint (workflow) definitions

## Sharing and moving projects

Because Papyrus references PDFs by their file path, move the project file together with its PDFs to keep everything linked. Alternatively, use **Configuration Packs** to export settings and templates for sharing with collaborators.

title: Importing and Managing Documents
summary: How to add, remove, rename, and organise PDFs in your project.
body:
# Importing Documents

Add PDFs to your project to read, annotate, and analyse them.

## Add a PDF

- Click the **Add PDF** button in the toolbar, or
- Drag one or more PDF files directly onto the **Document Explorer** on the left sidebar.

Once added, the document appears in the explorer list. Click it to open it in the viewer.

## Bulk import

Drag multiple PDFs at once onto the explorer list. Papyrus imports them all in one step.

## Removing a document

Right-click the document in the explorer and choose **Remove from Project**. This removes the reference from your project; it does not delete the original file from disk.

## Renaming a document

Right-click a document → **Rename** to give it a friendlier display name within Papyrus.

## Filtering the document list

Use the **Tag Filter** dropdown at the top of the explorer to show only documents that have been assigned certain tags.

## Scanned PDFs (no selectable text)

If a PDF is a scanned image with no embedded text, Papyrus cannot search or analyse it until you run OCR:
1. Right-click the document in the explorer.
2. Choose **Run OCR**.
3. Papyrus extracts text using optical character recognition and stores the result.

See the **OCR** help topic for more details.

## Supported formats

Papyrus supports many source formats beyond PDF — Word, EPUB, plain text, Markdown, HTML, RTF, CSV/TSV, Excel, video, audio, and images — all with the same highlighting, notes, AI analysis, search, and jump-to-source features. See the **Supported Source Formats** help topic for the full list and any per-format caveats.

title: Highlighting Text
summary: How to highlight passages in a PDF and manage highlight colours.
body:
# Highlighting Text

Highlights let you mark important passages in any PDF. They are saved in your project and can be tagged, colour-coded, and linked to notes.

## Create a highlight

1. Click and drag in the PDF viewer to select text.
2. Right-click the selection to open the context menu.
3. Hover over **Highlight** to see the colour submenu.
4. Choose a colour: **Yellow**, **Green**, **Blue**, **Purple**, or **Red**.

The highlight is immediately saved to your project.

## Change a highlight colour

- Click an existing highlight to select it.
- The colour picker appears (five coloured buttons).
- Click a different colour button to change it.

## Delete a highlight

- Select a highlight and press **Delete**, or
- Click the **✖** button on the highlight's popup card in the Notes dock.

## Assign tags to a highlight

Right-click a highlight → **Manage Tags** to assign or remove tags. Tagged highlights can be filtered in the Notes dock.

## Add a note to a highlight

Click a highlight and type in the note field that appears. Notes are displayed in the **Notes dock** alongside the highlighted text. See the **Annotation Notes** topic for more.

## Colour meanings

You can use colours however you like. A common convention:
- 🟡 **Yellow** — general interest
- 🟢 **Green** — supporting evidence
- 🔵 **Blue** — key definitions
- 🟣 **Purple** — counterarguments
- 🔴 **Red** — critical / flag for follow-up

## Viewing all highlights

The **Notes dock** lists every highlight in the current document (or the whole project). Use the scope dropdown to switch between *Current PDF* and *Entire Project*.

title: Annotation Notes
summary: How to write notes attached to highlights or PDF passages.
body:
# Annotation Notes

You can attach a written note to any highlight. Notes appear in the **Notes dock** and can be filtered, tagged, and colour-coded.

## Write a note

1. Create a highlight (select text → right-click → Highlight).
2. Click the highlight to open it.
3. Type your note in the text field that appears.
4. Press **Enter** or click outside to save.

## AI-generated notes

AI tools can automatically generate notes on your highlights or document passages. These appear in the Notes dock with an **AI** badge.

## Note types in the Notes dock

- **User Notes** — written by you.
- **AI Notes** — generated by AI tools.
- **Discovered Entities** — entities extracted from document analysis. These have a special card with:
  - Entity type and source document
  - Context paragraph with the relevant text highlighted
  - **Jump to Source (↗️)** — navigate to the page where the entity was found
  - **Edit & Save (✏️)** — modify the entity text and context
  - **Reject (✖)** — remove the entity from your analysis results

## Filter notes

- **Scope dropdown**: Show notes from *Current PDF* or *Entire Project*.
- **Tag filter**: Show only notes assigned to specific tags.

## Change a note's colour

In the Notes dock, use the five colour buttons at the bottom of a note card to change its colour.

## Delete a note

Click the **✖** button on the note card in the Notes dock.

title: OCR — Extracting Text from Scanned PDFs
summary: Use OCR to make scanned or image-only PDFs searchable and analysable.
body:
# OCR (Optical Character Recognition)

If a PDF was created by scanning physical pages, it contains images rather than selectable text. Papyrus cannot search, highlight, or analyse image-only PDFs until OCR has been run.

## Run OCR on a document

1. Right-click the document in the **Document Explorer** (left sidebar).
2. Choose **Run OCR**.
3. Papyrus OCRs only the pages that have no usable text, several pages at a time, and adds an invisible searchable text layer. The page images are not changed, so highlights stay where they are.

OCR takes roughly 1–3 seconds per page per CPU core; a 400-page scan takes several minutes. You can cancel it.

## The OCR engine

OCR uses **Tesseract**. If it is not installed, open **Settings → AI Setup → Pipeline Models → OCR engine (Tesseract)** and click **Install**. On Linux your desktop asks for the administrator password; on macOS Homebrew is used and on Windows winget.

## After OCR

- Text becomes selectable in the PDF viewer.
- The document can now be indexed for AI chat and analysis.
- Existing analysis templates can be run on the extracted text.

## Quality notes

OCR accuracy depends on scan quality. A clean, high-resolution scan gives near-perfect results. Low-resolution or skewed scans may contain errors. You can edit extracted text if needed.

## Re-running OCR

You can run OCR again on the same document if you want to refresh the extracted text (for example, after getting a higher-quality scan).

## Accessing OCR from the toolbar

You can also open the OCR tool directly from **Toolbar → Other Tools → OCR**.

title: Why Intelligence Asks for OCR
summary: Scanned PDFs are checked before any intelligence runs; when they have no usable text you are offered OCR in one click.
body:
# Why intelligence asks for OCR

Every intelligence run starts by parsing the document's text. Before parsing a PDF, Papyrus samples its pages (up to 40, spread through the document) and checks the text layer:

- **Scanned pages** — pages that are images with no text.
- **Garbled pages** — text that extracts as symbols or broken characters (damaged fonts or a poor earlier OCR).

If a quarter or more of the pages with content fail the check, or no text is found at all, the **parsed blocks** stage is marked **blocked — Needs OCR** and every later stage waits. Nothing is reported as complete with empty results.

## The OCR prompt

When this happens a prompt opens:

- **Install OCR engine** — shown when Tesseract is missing. It uses your system package manager (you approve the permission prompt).
- **Run OCR now** — adds a text layer to the same file. Original page images are kept. Intelligence restarts automatically when OCR finishes.
- **OCR to a new copy** — writes `name_ocr.pdf` next to the original and adds it to the project; the copy is processed as a new source.
- **Not now** — close the prompt. The document stays blocked; running intelligence again shows the prompt again.

## Images

Image sources are OCR'd during parsing. If the engine is missing, the prompt offers only the install, then processes the image again.

## Large documents

The check reads text only, so it is fast even for very large files. OCR itself is the slow part: it runs on several pages in parallel and can be cancelled from the prompt.

title: Chat with Your Documents
summary: Ask questions and have a conversation with an AI that has access to all your project documents.
body:
# Chat with Your Documents

The **Chat tab** (💬) in the Research dock lets you have a multi-turn conversation with an AI assistant that can search and quote from all the documents in your project.

## Opening Chat

1. Click the **Research Assistant** button in the toolbar to open the Research dock.
2. Select the **💬 Chat** tab.

## Asking a question

1. Type your question in the input field at the bottom.
2. Press **Enter** or click the **Send** button.
3. The AI responds with an answer and inline **citation bubbles** showing the exact passages from your documents it used.

Citation bubbles show the source document name, page number, and quoted text. Click a citation to jump to that page in the PDF viewer.

## Chat history

Your conversation is saved automatically in the project. When you reopen the project, your previous chat session is restored. Use the **Clear Chat History** button to start a fresh conversation.

## Streamed responses

Responses appear word-by-word as the AI generates them — you don't need to wait for the full answer.

## Controlling which documents the AI uses

By default, the AI searches all indexed documents. To limit context to specific PDFs or tags, click the **Settings (⚙️)** button next to the input field. This opens the **Context Filter** — see the *Controlling AI Context* topic for details.

## Viewing the prompts used

Every AI response has a **View Prompt Trace** button. Click it to inspect the exact system prompt and retrieved document chunks that were sent to the AI model. This is useful for debugging or understanding why an answer was given.

## Tips

- Ask follow-up questions — the AI remembers the conversation.
- Be specific: "What does Smith argue about carbon pricing in Chapter 3?" outperforms "Tell me about carbon."
- If an answer seems wrong, check the citations — the AI may have retrieved an unrelated passage.
- Use the **Brainstorm** tab (💡) for creative ideation instead of factual Q&A.

title: Controlling AI Context (Context Filter)
summary: Choose which documents and tags the AI searches when answering your questions.
body:
# Controlling AI Context

By default, the Chat and Brainstorm AI searches all documents in your project. The **Context Filter** lets you narrow this to specific PDFs or tagged groups.

## Opening the Context Filter

Click the **⚙️ Settings** button next to the chat input field.

## Document filter

Select one or more documents from the list. The AI will only retrieve passages from the documents you select. Leave all unchecked to search everything.

## Tag filter

Select one or more tags. The AI will only retrieve passages from documents that have been assigned those tags.

## Tag logic (AND / OR)

When you select multiple tags, use the toggle to choose:
- **OR** — retrieve passages from documents with *any* of the selected tags.
- **AND** — retrieve passages only from documents that have *all* of the selected tags.

## Saving context settings

Your filter settings are saved automatically to the project metadata. They persist between sessions.

## Typical uses

- **Focused analysis**: Select only the three papers relevant to your current question.
- **Topic clusters**: Tag all papers on a topic, then filter by that tag so the AI focuses on that cluster.
- **Cross-document comparison**: Select exactly two documents to ask the AI to compare them directly.

## Active context indicator

When a context filter is active, the Settings button shows a visual indicator so you always know the AI's context is restricted.

title: Brainstorm — Generate Ideas from Your Research
summary: Use the Brainstorm tab to synthesise ideas, arguments, and hypotheses from your documents.
body:
# Brainstorm Tab

The **Brainstorm tab** (💡) is designed for creative synthesis. Unlike the Chat tab which answers specific questions, Brainstorm generates new ideas, arguments, and possibilities by combining what it finds in your documents with open-ended AI reasoning.

## Opening Brainstorm

Research dock → **💡 Brainstorm** tab.

## Strategy modes

Choose a strategy from the dropdown before submitting:

### 1. Creative Synthesis (default)
Minimal document constraints — the AI generates ideas freely, optionally inspired by your documents. Best for early-stage ideation or when you want to think beyond what the documents say.

### 2. RAG + Creative Expansion
Balanced mode. The AI retrieves relevant passages from your documents and then expands on them creatively. Good for building on existing evidence while exploring new angles.

### 3. Strict Document Evidence Only
The AI only quotes and synthesises what it can directly find in your documents. No creative extrapolation. Best for summarisation tasks or when you need to stay tightly grounded in the source material.

## How to brainstorm

1. Select a strategy mode.
2. Type your thesis, question, or topic into the input field.
   - Example: *"What are the strongest counterarguments to the privatisation of water utilities?"*
   - Example: *"Generate 5 novel research hypotheses from these climate papers."*
3. Click **Send**.

## Reading results

Results stream in with ideas numbered or bulleted. Each idea may include citation bubbles linking back to your documents.

## Tips

- Phrase your input as a directive: *"Generate"*, *"List"*, *"Compare"*, *"Argue for"*.
- Use **Strict Document Evidence Only** when you want the AI to act as a structured summariser.
- Use **Creative Synthesis** when you're stuck and need inspiration beyond what the papers say.

title: Running Document Analysis
summary: Use AI analysis templates to extract structured information — claims, entities, methods — from your PDFs.
body:
# Document Analysis

The **Analysis tab** (🔬) in the Research dock uses AI to read your PDF and extract structured information as a graph of nodes and relationships. The template you choose determines what the AI looks for.

## Running an analysis

1. Open a PDF in the viewer.
2. Go to the Research dock → **🔬 Analysis** tab.
3. Select a document from the **Document** dropdown (defaults to the open document).
4. Choose an **analysis template** from the mode dropdown.
5. Click **▶ Run Analysis**.

Papyrus splits the document into chunks and sends each to the AI in parallel. Results stream back chunk by chunk. For long documents this may take 1–3 minutes.

## What you see during analysis

Each chunk produces a **result card** showing:
- Number of nodes, edges, and quotes extracted from that chunk
- A preview of the extracted entities
- A **View Prompt Trace** button — click to see the exact prompt sent to the AI
- A **Send to Workspace** button — add these nodes to the visual Workspace canvas

## Reviewing results

Switch to the **Review & Synthesise** sub-tab to browse all saved analysis results for a document:

- **Sections view**: Each chunk listed with expandable details (claims, quotes, reasoning).
- **Master Outline view**: A synthesised summary combining all chunks into a unified structure.
- **Compare Outlines view**: Select two documents to see an AI-generated comparison of their analysis results.

## Re-running with a different template

You can run multiple templates on the same document. Results from different templates are stored separately and do not overwrite each other.

## Sending results to the Workspace

Click **Send to Workspace** on any result card to add the extracted nodes and edges to the visual Workspace canvas. From there you can arrange, connect, and explore them visually.

## Tips

- Run **Argument Map** on argumentative texts (papers, essays).
- Run **Relationship Network** on texts about people, organisations, or events.
- Run **Methodology Tracker** on empirical research papers to extract study steps.
- For very long documents, the analysis runs faster if you only send specific pages by using the page range setting.

title: Built-in Analysis Templates
summary: What each built-in template extracts and when to use it.
body:
# Built-in Analysis Templates

Templates define what the AI extracts from your document and how it structures the results. Choose one from the dropdown in the Analysis tab before running.

## Argument Map

**Best for**: Academic papers, essays, opinion pieces, legal documents.

Extracts:
- **Claims** — main assertions made by the author.
- **Reasoning pillars** — supporting arguments for each claim.
- **Evidence / Quotes** — direct quotations that back up each argument.
- **Relationships**: *supports*, *refutes*, *part_of*, *derived_from*.

The result is a hierarchical map of the text's argumentative structure — ideal for seeing how conclusions are justified.

## Methodology Tracker

**Best for**: Empirical research papers, scientific studies, technical reports.

Extracts:
- **Method steps** — individual steps of the research methodology in order.
- **Findings** — results corresponding to each step.
- **Limitations** — caveats and constraints noted by the authors.
- **Relationships**: *next_step*, *produces*, *supports*, *contradicts*.

Useful for quickly understanding how a study was designed and what it found.

## Relationship / Network Tracker

**Best for**: Biographical texts, historical documents, organisational analyses, news articles.

Extracts:
- **People** — named individuals.
- **Organisations** — companies, institutions, groups.
- **Affiliations** — who belongs to or works for what.
- **Events** — significant happenings linking entities.
- **Relationships**: *affiliated_with*, *opposes*, *collaborated_with*, *led_by*.

Builds a social or organisational network you can explore in the Workspace.

## Template details

Each template specifies:
- Which node types the AI may create
- Which relationship types are allowed
- Per-chunk token limits and maximum entity counts
- The specific system prompts used at chunk-level and master-synthesis level

See **Creating Custom Templates** to build your own.

title: Creating Custom Analysis Templates
summary: Build your own analysis templates to extract exactly what you need from your documents.
body:
# Creating Custom Analysis Templates

Open Research → Analysis → Edit Modes (Modes Builder). Create a mode or select a saved mode, enter its title and analysis goal, then check its node and connection vocabulary. Save once the validation preview reports a compatible vocabulary.

## Node and connection choices

Choices come from the application's live ontology, including installed plugins. Check the types your graph may use. A connection must permit at least one pair of the selected node types. For example, Reasons For needs a Reasoning source; choosing only Claim and Quote makes that connection incompatible. The preview explains the problem and disables Save.

Checked vocabulary restricts the default graph vocabulary. Quote keeps the source-backed quote renderer. Defining a new type requires a registered plugin/type implementation; typing an invented name into instructions does not create it.

An unavailable legacy/plugin name stays visible as a checked Unavailable entry. Uncheck and replace it deliberately, or restore its plugin. Invalid saved modes are explained near the mode picker; they do not hide other valid modes.

## Analysis goal and quote selection

Describe the research question and the relationships you want to examine. Instructions guide the shared analysis workflow; they do not establish that an extraction or connection is correct.

Quotes per section, relevant sections and total evidence quotes bound the evidence packet. Canonical quotation text remains complete and source-backed. Target/max quote-word and explanation-word controls, and the Legacy Chunk Workflow Pre-Filters group, apply to older chunk workflows. Current artifact analysis uses shared focus filtering and canonical classifications instead of those pre-filters. Shared prompts remain editable through Advanced: Edit Shared Prompts.

## Preparation requirements

The preview explains the mode's preparation stages and required artifacts. Requirements can distinguish all from any artifact types, across the selected sources or within each source. The same source-category planner and artifact eligibility checks run after preparation, before inference. A completed Dates pass may find zero dates and still yield a valid empty timeline.

Use **Required intelligence** to choose processing passes and add or remove artifact requirement groups. Every group must pass. **All selected types** requires every checked artifact type; **Any selected type** requires at least one. **Across selected sources** allows the selection to satisfy the group together; **In each selected source** requires each source to qualify independently. Stage dependencies adapt to source category through the shared planner. Hover an artifact type to see which registered passes produce it. Selecting a type does not silently check another processing pass.

Removing every group means no required-artifact gate; unchecking every pass means no automatic preparation. Neither setting means the source contains a useful argument. Existing current artifacts are still eligible. Missing prerequisite metadata in older modes retains the documented legacy defaults.

Unavailable or disabled saved plugin types/passes remain visibly selected. Restore their provider or explicitly remove/replace them before saving. Invalid saved groups can be corrected or explicitly removed. The shared typed form, backend readiness and saved settings use the same policy.

**Graph and evidence** contains active quote-per-section, section and total candidate caps, including one section/one quote. Preview and saved contracts reflect these values and the current research goal. Whole canonical quotations stay verbatim. Invalid saved active caps require explicit replacement.

**Legacy workflows** contains word targets, fallback text and chunk pre-filters. These do not reclassify or shorten canonical artifacts in the new graph pipeline. Existing custom model limits and prompt keys are preserved when editing. Option pages scroll inside the resizable builder; prerequisite controls link to this help topic.

## Coverage and current limits

Canonical artifacts form the baseline. The model can suggest bounded label/statement changes and relations over existing nodes; those connections remain unreviewed. Missing evidence or connections remain a partial analysis. A valid vocabulary is not a guarantee of semantic quality.

Current analysis projections cover canonical argument units and an independent user-focus root. A template requesting method steps, people or time periods does not automatically extract or generate those nodes. General custom-node/stance projections, exact serialized provider context budgets and live-model quality/recovery qualification remain in progress. Some bundled legacy templates reference unregistered vocabulary; their reported errors must be corrected explicitly rather than silently substituted.

title: The Knowledge Workspace
summary: Navigate the visual canvas where analysis results, highlights, and ideas connect into a knowledge graph.
body:
# The Knowledge Workspace

The **Workspace** is a visual, interactive canvas where nodes represent ideas, claims, entities, or findings, and edges (arrows) represent the relationships between them. Analysis results appear here automatically when you click *Send to Workspace*.

## Opening the Workspace

Click **Workspace** in the toolbar or side panel. You can have multiple named workspaces — switch between them using the workspace selector dropdown at the top of the Workspace dock.

## Navigating the canvas

- **Scroll** — zoom in and out.
- **Middle-click drag** (or two-finger drag on a trackpad) — pan the canvas.
- **Click a node** — select it and show its properties in the side panel.
- **Double-click a node** — open the full node editor.
- **Ctrl+A** — select all nodes.
- **Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y** — undo / redo.

## Understanding nodes

Each node has:
- **Title** — the main label shown on the canvas.
- **Type** — colour-coded by entity type (Claim = orange, Quote = teal, Method = blue, etc.).
- **Description / body** — detailed text visible when expanded.
- **Tags** — organisational tags assignable from the context menu.
- **Source document** — the PDF and page number the node came from (if extracted from analysis).

## Understanding edges

Edges (arrows) represent relationships. Common types:
- *supports* — one claim supports another
- *refutes* / *contradicts* — opposing relationship
- *part_of* — hierarchy or containment
- *derived_from* — one idea built on another
- *next_step* — sequential flow

Right-click an edge to edit or delete it.

## Creating nodes and edges manually

- **Right-click the canvas** → **Add Node** to create a node from scratch.
- **Drag from a node's edge port** to another node to draw a relationship arrow.

## Workspace selector

Use the **dropdown at the top of the Workspace dock** to switch between:
- **Main Board** — the default workspace.
- Any custom workspaces you have created.

To create a new workspace, click the **+ New Workspace** button.

## Filters

- **PDF filter** — show only nodes extracted from a specific document.
- **Tag filter** — show only nodes with certain tags assigned.

Filters do not delete nodes; they temporarily hide unmatched ones.

## Layout tools

Right-click the canvas → **Auto-arrange** to apply an automatic force-directed layout. Zoom and pan controls are also available in the toolbar above the canvas.

title: Working with Nodes and Edges
summary: Create, edit, connect, and delete nodes and edges in the Workspace canvas.
body:
# Nodes and Edges

## Editing a node

1. Double-click any node to open the **Node Editor**.
2. Change the **title**, **description**, **type**, or **tags**.
3. Click **Save**.

## Moving nodes

Click and drag any node to reposition it on the canvas. Hold **Shift** to snap to a grid.

## Selecting multiple nodes

- Click an empty area and drag to draw a selection box.
- Hold **Ctrl** and click to add/remove individual nodes from the selection.
- **Ctrl+A** to select everything.

## Copying and pasting

- Select nodes and press **Ctrl+C** to copy.
- Press **Ctrl+V** to paste. Edges between the copied nodes are preserved.

## Drawing an edge

1. Hover over a node until you see a small **port circle** appear on its edge.
2. Click and drag from that port to another node.
3. A **New Edge** dialog appears — choose a relationship type.
4. Click **Create** to confirm.

## Editing an edge

Right-click an edge arrow → **Edit Edge** to change the relationship type or direction.

## Deleting nodes and edges

- Select nodes and press **Delete** or **Backspace**.
- Right-click a node or edge → **Delete**.

## Node types and colours

Each analysis template defines its own node types, each with a unique colour. The legend appears in the Workspace toolbar. Common types:

| Type | Typical colour |
|---|---|
| entity.claim | Orange |
| entity.quote | Teal |
| entity.finding | Green |
| entity.method | Blue |
| entity.person | Purple |
| entity.org | Red |

## Collapsing and expanding nodes

For a cleaner canvas, click a node's collapse button (▼) to hide its body text and shrink it to a chip. Click again (▶) to expand.

## Generating an outline from selected nodes

Select nodes → right-click → **Generate Outline**. Papyrus creates a hierarchical text outline from the selected portion of your graph.

title: AI Tools in the Workspace
summary: Let the AI analyse, organise, and summarise your knowledge graph.
body:
# AI Tools in the Workspace

The Workspace includes several AI-powered tools that operate on the nodes and edges already in your graph.

## Accessing AI tools

Right-click the canvas (or select nodes and right-click) to see the AI actions menu. You can also find them in the Workspace toolbar.

## Find Weakpoints

Analyses the graph and highlights **unsupported claims** — nodes that make assertions but have no supporting evidence or citation edges.

Results appear in a **Weakpoints Dialog** listing each flagged node, the reason it was flagged, and suggestions for what evidence to look for.

Useful for: checking argument maps before writing a paper, identifying gaps in a literature review.

## Color Organise by Theme

The AI reads all node titles and descriptions, clusters them into semantic themes, and recolours nodes by theme. Each cluster gets a unique colour, making thematic patterns visually obvious at a glance.

Use this after importing a large analysis to quickly see which ideas cluster together.

## Generate Outline

Select a set of nodes → right-click → **Generate Outline**.

Papyrus sends the selected nodes (with their edges) to the AI, which produces a hierarchical textual outline ordered by logical flow. The outline is displayed in a dialog and can be copied to the clipboard.

Useful for: drafting an essay structure from a research graph, creating a presentation outline.

## Declutter & Simplify

Opens the **Declutter Settings** dialog where you can:
- Merge semantically duplicate nodes into one.
- Remove low-confidence edges.
- Simplify long node titles.
- Apply automatic layout after cleanup.

## Outline Workspace Graph

A full-graph version of Generate Outline — considers all nodes on the canvas, not just a selection.

## Tips

- Run **Color Organise** after a large multi-document analysis to see cross-document themes.
- Use **Find Weakpoints** before writing to identify where you need more evidence.
- **Generate Outline** then copy the result into your writing tool to scaffold a first draft.

title: Blueprint Editor — Building Custom Workflows
summary: Design reusable AI workflows by connecting action nodes in the Blueprint Editor.
body:
# Blueprint Editor

The **Blueprint Editor** (🛠️) lets you build programmable AI workflows — called **blueprints** — without writing code. A blueprint is a graph of connected action nodes; when you run it, each node executes in order, passing its output to the next.

Blueprints can be saved as **Custom Tools**, which then appear in the **🧰 Custom Tools** tab for one-click execution.

## Opening the Blueprint Editor

Research dock → **🛠️ Blueprint Editor** tab.

## The interface

- **Left canvas** — the visual node graph where you design your workflow.
- **Right panel, AI Builder tab** — a chat interface where you describe what you want the AI to build for you.
- **Right panel, Debugger tab** — run and step through your blueprint to test it.
- **Bottom bar** — Add Node, Auto-Link Selected, Save Blueprint buttons, plus Name and Description fields.
- **Top bar** — New Tool (✨), Restore Default, Delete, Docs & Help (❓), and the Target Blueprint selector dropdown.

## Creating a blueprint

### Option A: Use the AI Builder Assistant

1. Switch to the **AI Builder** tab in the right panel.
2. Describe your workflow in plain English. For example:
   > *"Search my documents for any mention of climate policy, then summarise all findings in bullet points."*
3. The AI generates the blueprint JSON and renders it on the canvas automatically.
4. Review the nodes, adjust any parameters, then click **Save Blueprint**.

### Option B: Build manually on the canvas

1. Click **+ Add Node** in the bottom bar.
2. Select a node type (LLM Query, RAG Search, Python Script, Branch, For Each — see *Blueprint Node Types*).
3. Configure the node's parameters in the properties panel.
4. Repeat and connect nodes by dragging from one node's output port to another's input port.
5. Name the blueprint in the Name field and click **Save Blueprint**.

## Running and testing

1. In the Debugger tab, click **Run Test in Debugger**.
2. Papyrus executes the blueprint step by step, showing the state (all variable values) after each node.
3. Any errors appear in the terminal-style output at the bottom.

## Saving as a Custom Tool

Once saved, your blueprint appears in the **🧰 Custom Tools** tab dropdown. Other users with the same project can run it immediately.

## Editing an existing tool

Select the blueprint from the Target Blueprint dropdown at the top of the editor, make your changes, and click **Save**.

## Restoring defaults

Click **Restore Default** to revert any built-in blueprint to its factory state. This only affects built-in tools, not ones you created.

title: Blueprint Node Types
summary: A guide to every type of node you can add to a blueprint workflow.
body:
# Blueprint Node Types

Each node in a blueprint performs a specific action. Connect nodes to build a pipeline where the output of one step feeds into the next.

## LLM Query

**What it does**: Sends a prompt to an AI language model and stores the response in a state variable.

**Configure**:
- **Prompt template**: The text sent to the AI. Use `{variable_name}` placeholders to inject values from previous steps.
- **System message**: Optional system role text.
- **Output variable**: The state variable name where the response is stored.
- **Model**: Choose which AI model to use for this step (can differ from other nodes).

**Example**: An LLM Query node with the prompt `"Summarise the following in 3 bullet points: {rag_results}"` takes RAG output and condenses it.

## RAG Search

**What it does**: Searches your indexed documents using semantic similarity and stores matching passages in a state variable.

**Configure**:
- **Query**: The search query. Usually `{user_input}` or a previous LLM output.
- **Max chunks**: How many document chunks to retrieve (default: 5).
- **Document filter**: Optionally restrict which documents are searched.
- **Output variable**: Where to store the retrieved passages.

## Python Script

**What it does**: Runs a small Python function inline.

**Configure**:
- **Script**: Python code with access to the current blueprint state as a dictionary (`state`).
- Must return a dict of variable updates.
- Has access to `analysis_api` and `normalize_graph_object` helper functions.

**Example**:
```python
results = state.get('rag_results', '')
words = len(results.split())
return {'word_count': words}
```

**Safety**: Scripts run in a restricted environment. File system and network access are not available.

## Branch / Condition

**What it does**: Routes execution to different downstream nodes based on a condition.

**Configure**:
- **Condition**: A Python expression evaluated against the current state. For example: `state['word_count'] > 500`.
- **True branch**: The node to execute if the condition is true.
- **False branch**: The node to execute if the condition is false.

## For Each

**What it does**: Loops over a list stored in a state variable and runs a sub-pipeline for each item.

**Configure**:
- **List variable**: The state variable containing the list to iterate.
- **Item variable**: The name given to each item as it enters the loop body.
- **Body**: Connect nodes inside the loop.

## Output Formats

Some nodes produce structured output. The `output_format` field controls how results are routed:
- `text` — plain text, shown in the results console.
- `graph` — a node/edge graph, added to the Workspace.
- `json` — raw JSON, available for downstream nodes.
- `markdown` — formatted text.

## Auto-Link Selected

Select two or more nodes in the order you want them to run, then click **Auto-Link Selected** in the bottom bar. Papyrus draws edges between them automatically.

title: Variables and State in Blueprints
summary: How state variables flow through a blueprint and how to use built-in variables.
body:
# Variables and State in Blueprints

Blueprints use a **state dictionary** — a set of named variables that is passed from node to node. Each node can read from and write to this dictionary.

## Referencing variables in prompts

In any text field (prompt template, system message, query), use curly braces to inject a variable value:

```
Summarise the following passages: {rag_results}
```

If `rag_results` is in the state, its value is substituted. If it is missing, the placeholder is left blank (or triggers an error depending on the node's settings).

## Built-in variables

These variables are automatically set at the start of every blueprint run:

| Variable | Contents |
|---|---|
| `{user_input}` | The text typed by the user in the Custom Tools input field |
| `{document_text}` | The full extracted text of the currently open document |
| `{selected_text}` | Text currently selected in the PDF viewer (if any) |
| `{project_name}` | The name of the current project |
| `{doc_title}` | The title of the currently open document |

## Setting variables from nodes

Every node has an **Output variable** field. The node's result is stored under that name. Subsequent nodes can read it.

Example pipeline:
1. **RAG Search** → output variable: `rag_results`
2. **LLM Query** → prompt: `"Based on: {rag_results}, answer: {user_input}"` → output: `answer`
3. **LLM Query** → prompt: `"Make this concise: {answer}"` → output: `summary`

## Expected inputs (dynamic forms)

You can declare `expected_inputs` in the blueprint definition to create a form that appears in the Custom Tools tab before the user runs the tool:

```json
"expected_inputs": [
  {"name": "research_topic", "type": "text_long", "label": "Research topic"},
  {"name": "target_doc",     "type": "doc_selector", "label": "Document to analyse"}
]
```

Input types: `text_long`, `text_short`, `dropdown`, `doc_selector`.

## State inspection in the Debugger

When you run a blueprint in the Debugger (right panel → Debugger tab), the full state dictionary is shown after each node executes. This lets you verify that variables contain what you expect before continuing to the next step.

title: AI Builder Assistant for Blueprints
summary: Describe a workflow in plain English and let the AI build the blueprint for you.
body:
# AI Builder Assistant

The **AI Builder Assistant** is a chat interface inside the Blueprint Editor that lets you describe a workflow in natural language. The AI generates the blueprint automatically — no manual node placement needed.

## Opening the AI Builder

1. Go to Research dock → **🛠️ Blueprint Editor** tab.
2. In the right panel, select the **AI Builder** tab.

## How to use it

1. Type a description of the workflow you want. Be specific about:
   - What information you're starting with (user input, a document, selected text)
   - What steps should happen
   - What the final output should look like

2. The AI responds with a generated blueprint and renders it on the left canvas in real time.

3. Review the generated nodes. You can:
   - Accept it as-is and click **Save Blueprint**.
   - Ask follow-up questions to refine it: *"Make the summary shorter"*, *"Add a step that filters results to only include claims about legislation"*.
   - Manually edit individual nodes on the canvas.

## Example prompts

> *"Search my documents for any mention of the Paris Agreement, then write a 200-word summary of what they say, formatted as markdown."*

> *"For each document in my project, extract the main conclusion and store them all in a list."*

> *"Ask the user what topic they want to explore, search the project for relevant passages, then generate 5 research questions based on what you find."*

## Iterating

You can have a multi-turn conversation with the builder:
- *"The search step should only look at documents tagged 'climate'."*
- *"Add an input that lets the user choose how many bullet points they want."*
- *"Rename the output variable to 'final_answer'."*

Each refinement updates the canvas immediately.

## Saving

Once satisfied, name the blueprint in the bottom bar and click **Save Blueprint**. It will appear in the Custom Tools tab.

body:

title: The Research Agent
summary: An autonomous multi-step AI agent that plans and executes complex research tasks.
body:
# Research Agent

The **Research Agent** (🧭) is an autonomous AI that breaks a complex research goal into steps, executes them one at a time using your documents and AI tools, and reports what it finds at each stage.

Unlike the Chat tab (single question → single answer), the Research Agent plans a multi-step strategy and carries it out — stopping to show you progress and ask for direction at key moments.

## Opening the Research Agent

Research dock → **🧭 Research Agent** tab.

## Starting a research session

1. Type your research goal in the input field. Be as specific as you can:
   - *"Find the five strongest pieces of evidence supporting the hypothesis that X causes Y across all my documents."*
   - *"Summarise how different authors in this project disagree about the role of regulation in innovation."*
2. Click **▶ Start**.

## What happens

1. The agent **plans**: it decides what searches to run, what questions to ask, and in what order.
2. It **executes each step** sequentially, showing you what it's doing and what it found.
3. It **reports artifacts** — search results, summaries, extracted facts — as it proceeds.
4. It **pauses for input** at key decision points. You can approve the plan, add instructions, or redirect it.

## Controls

- **▶ Start / Send** — launch or send a follow-up instruction.
- **Continue** — let the agent proceed to the next planned step without adding new instructions.
- **New** — reset the session and start fresh.

## Session persistence

The agent's session state is saved to your project. If you close and reopen Papyrus, you can pick up where you left off.

## Status indicators

The **Status Pill** at the top shows: *Idle*, *Planning*, or *Executing*.

## Tips

- Give the agent a clear goal with a defined output: *"...and produce a 3-paragraph summary of your findings."*
- After the agent reports a plan, review it before clicking **Continue** — you can redirect it: *"Skip the third step and focus on the comparative analysis instead."*
- The agent performs best on goals that benefit from multi-step searching and synthesis, not simple factual questions (use Chat for those).

title: Tags — Organising Documents, Highlights, and Nodes

body:
# Tags

Tags are coloured labels you can assign to documents, highlights, notes, and workspace nodes. They let you filter and group information across your entire project.

## Creating tags

1. Click the **Tag Manager (🏷️)** button in the toolbar.
2. Click **+ New Tag**.
3. Enter a name and choose a colour.
4. Click **Save**.

## Assigning tags

### To a document
- Right-click a document in the Document Explorer → **Assign Tags**.

### To a highlight or note
- Right-click a highlight in the PDF viewer → **Manage Tags**.
- Or click the tag dot on a note card in the Notes dock → **Manage Tags**.

### To a workspace node

- **Notes dock**: Use the Tag Filter dropdown.

title: How AI Works in Papyrus
summary: Understand how Papyrus uses LLMs, RAG, and what happens when you run an AI feature.
body:
# How AI Works in Papyrus

Papyrus uses Large Language Models (LLMs) such as Claude (Anthropic) or GPT-4 (OpenAI) to power every AI feature. Understanding the basic pipeline helps you get better results.

## Setting up your AI model

1. Click the **Settings (⚙️)** button in the toolbar.
2. Enter your API key (Anthropic, OpenAI, or another supported provider).
3. Select a default model for chat, analysis, and other features.

You can select different models for different features (for example, a fast model for chat and a more powerful model for analysis).

## What is RAG?

**Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)** is the technique Papyrus uses so the AI can answer questions about your specific documents.

When you ask a question or run an analysis:
1. Papyrus **splits your documents into chunks** and indexes them using vector embeddings.
2. It **searches the index** for the chunks most relevant to your query.
3. The most relevant chunks are **included in the prompt** sent to the AI model.
4. The AI **generates a response** grounded in those retrieved passages.

This means the AI's answers are based on your actual documents, not just its training data.

## What is an index?

When you add a document to your project and it has text (or you've run OCR), Papyrus automatically indexes it. The index is a vector database stored in your project file.

If a document is not appearing in AI responses, check that it has been indexed — you'll see an indicator in the Document Explorer.

## Models and their uses

- **Claude 3.5 Sonnet / Claude 3 Opus** — Recommended for deep analysis and complex reasoning.
- **Claude 3 Haiku** — Fast and cost-effective for simple summaries and chat.
- **GPT-4o / GPT-4 Turbo** — Strong alternative for chat and analysis.

Configure which model is used for which feature in Settings.

## Costs

Each AI call consumes tokens from your API provider. Longer documents and more detailed prompts use more tokens. Monitor usage in your API provider's dashboard.

## Privacy

Your document text is sent to the AI provider's API when you use AI features. Review your provider's data handling policies if you are working with sensitive documents.

title: Viewing the Prompts Sent to AI
summary: Use Prompt Trace to inspect every prompt, retrieved document chunk, and raw response for any AI output.
body:
# Prompt Tracing

**Prompt Trace** lets you see exactly what was sent to the AI model for any response — the full system prompt, the retrieved document chunks, any injected variables, and the raw model output. This is the most powerful tool for understanding and debugging AI behaviour in Papyrus.

## Where to find the Prompt Trace button

Every AI-generated output has a **View Prompt Trace** button:

- **Analysis result cards** — each chunk result in the Analysis tab has a *View Prompt Trace* button.
- **Chat messages** — each AI chat response has a Prompt Trace button (may appear on hover or in a message menu).
- **Custom Tool results** — the output panel shows a Prompt Trace link.

## What the trace shows

Clicking **View Prompt Trace** opens the Trace Viewer dialog containing:

- **System prompt** — the role definition and instructions given to the AI (from the Prompt Editor).
- **Retrieved chunks** — the exact document passages retrieved by RAG that were included in this call.
- **User message / injected variables** — what was substituted into the prompt template.
- **Full prompt JSON** — the complete API request in raw JSON format.
- **Token usage** — prompt tokens, completion tokens, and total cost estimate.
- **Raw response** — the model's unformatted output before Papyrus processed it.

## Why this is useful

- **Debugging wrong answers**: If the AI gave an incorrect answer, check which chunks were retrieved — it may have retrieved an irrelevant passage.
- **Understanding analysis results**: See exactly what instructions the analysis template gave the AI.
- **Prompt engineering**: Identify where a prompt can be improved and then edit it in the Prompt Editor.
- **Transparency**: Verify that the AI's reasoning is grounded in your actual documents.

## Enabling prompt tracing

Prompt tracing is on by default. You can toggle it in **Settings → AI → Save Prompt Traces**.

## Copying trace data

In the Trace Viewer, click **Copy to Clipboard** to copy the full trace as JSON for external analysis or bug reporting.

title: Editing AI Prompts
summary: Customise the system prompts that control how the AI behaves in every feature.
body:
# Prompt Editor

The **Prompt Editor** (🧠) in the toolbar lets you view and edit the system prompts used by every AI feature in Papyrus. If you find the AI's tone, format, or level of detail unsatisfactory, this is where you change it.

## Opening the Prompt Editor

Click the **🧠 Prompt Editor** button in the top toolbar.

## Available prompt keys

Each AI feature has one or more named prompt keys:

| Key | Used by |
|---|---|
| `chat_system_universal` | Chat tab (main conversation prompt) |
| `brainstorm_system_default` | Brainstorm tab, Creative Synthesis mode |
| `brainstorm_system_rag` | Brainstorm tab, RAG + Creative Expansion mode |
| `brainstorm_system_strict` | Brainstorm tab, Strict Document Evidence mode |
| `analysis_chunk_observations` | Per-chunk extraction prompt for all analysis templates |
| `analysis_master_synthesis` | Final synthesis prompt combining all chunks |
| `research_agent_planner` | Research Agent planning prompt |

Custom analysis templates reference their own keys if you created them.

## Editing a prompt

1. Select a prompt key from the list.
2. The current prompt text appears in the editor pane.
3. Make your changes.
4. Click **Save**. Changes take effect immediately on the next AI call.

## Variable placeholders

Prompts use `{variable_name}` placeholders that are filled at runtime:
- `{document_text}` — the document chunk being analysed
- `{user_query}` — the user's question
- `{rag_results}` — retrieved document passages
- `{chat_history}` — prior conversation turns

Do not remove required placeholders or the feature may fail.

## Restoring defaults

Click **Restore Default** next to any prompt to revert it to the Papyrus factory version.

## Tips

- Add domain-specific instructions: *"This is a corpus of legal case law. Extract entities using legal terminology."*
- Change the output format: *"Always respond in bullet points. Never use prose paragraphs."*
- Change the language: *"Always respond in French, regardless of the document language."*
- Test your edits with **Prompt Trace** to verify the system prompt is being sent as expected.

title: Search — Finding Information Inside and Outside Your Project
summary: Use the Search tab for local document search, AI-generated queries, and external academic sources.
body:
# Search Tab

The **Search tab** (🔍) in the Research dock lets you search across your documents with semantic search, and also query external academic databases.

## Opening Search

Research dock → **🔍 Search** tab.

## Local document search

1. Type a query in the search bar.
2. Click **RAG Search** (or press Enter).

Results appear as **Citation Cards** showing:
- Source document and page number
- The relevant passage (with your search terms highlighted)
- A relevance score

Click a Citation Card to jump to that page in the PDF viewer.

## External academic search

Use the quick-access buttons to search external sources:
- **JSTOR** — journal articles in humanities and social sciences
- **Google Scholar** — broad academic literature
- **Reddit** — community discussions
- **News** — recent news articles
- **Custom URL** — search any other source

## AI Query Generator

If you have a broad research goal, let the AI generate and execute searches for you:

title: Text-to-Speech (Audio)
summary: Convert any PDF pages to spoken audio with selectable voice and speed.
body:
# Text-to-Speech

The **Audio dock** (🔊) converts PDF text into spoken audio. Useful for listening to papers while away from a screen or for accessibility.

## Opening the Audio dock

Toolbar → **Other Tools → Audio**.

## Converting pages to audio

1. Set the **page range** using the *Pages [start] to [end]* spinboxes.
2. Check **Ignore Headers/Footers** if you want the AI to strip running headers and footers from the text (checked by default).
3. Click **⬇️ Pull Text** to extract text from the selected pages.
4. Review and edit the extracted text in the text editor if needed.
5. Choose a **voice** from the voice selector dropdown.
6. Select a **speed**: 1.0× Normal, 1.2× Fast, 1.5× Very Fast.
7. Click **Generate Audio**.

The audio file is generated and can be played back or saved.

## Editing text before synthesis

After clicking **Pull Text**, the extracted text appears in an editable area. You can:
- Remove sections you don't want read aloud.
- Correct OCR errors.
- Add pronunciation hints.

## Voice selection

Voices are provided by the TTS service configured in Settings. The available voices depend on your provider (e.g., ElevenLabs, OpenAI TTS, system voices).

## Tips

- For scanned PDFs, run **OCR** first (right-click the document in the explorer → Run OCR).
- Use a shorter page range for faster generation — a full 300-page book will take several minutes.
- **Ignore Headers/Footers** usually produces cleaner audio for academic papers.

# What's This? Mode

What's This? mode lets you click any control in Papyrus to instantly open its help topic in the Help Center.

## Activating What's This?

# Blueprint Editor

The Blueprint Editor lets you build powerful, multi-step AI pipelines visually. Each workflow is called a **blueprint** and consists of nodes connected by edges.

Research Assistant dock → Blueprint Editor tab.
